{"id": "40:16/q06", "question": "Whom does 'they' identify?", "turns_on": "Whether the local antecedent in 40:14 restricts the group or the scene denotes humanity generally.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q06/p1", "position": "The people raised and gathered from their graves.", "reasons": "Most accounts speak of people or all humanity at resurrection: Muqātil, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Kathīr, Elmalılı and Study Quran. Muqātil pictures them spread over earth like a stretched hide."}, {"id": "40:16/q06/p2", "position": "The pronoun refers specifically to the disbelievers mentioned in 40:14.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr traces the third-person pronoun to that antecedent."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q07", "question": "What does their being 'exposed' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether exposure names bodily emergence, unobstructed visibility, or disclosure of inner realities; Ālūsī objects to a purely disembodied account.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q07/p1", "position": "They emerge from their graves into open view.", "reasons": "Muqātil likens the spread earth to a stretched hide; al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Elmalılı and Study Quran explicitly mention graves. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī report emergence as one sense. Bursevī defines baraza as coming into open space after concealment."}, {"id": "40:16/q07/p2", "position": "They stand plainly visible, with no terrain, building, or cover shielding them.", "reasons": "Qatāda says no mountain or mud building screens them, reported by ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Durr. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and Ālūsī describe the level earth without hill or building; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds that sight and a caller's voice reach them. Al-Biqāʿī includes inward and outward exposure."}, {"id": "40:16/q07/p3", "position": "Their souls, deeds, inner states, and secrets become manifest, including to one another.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says hidden states are disclosed and people see one another; al-Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī report disclosure of souls, deeds and secrets. Al-Biqāʿī calls exposure outward and inward; Iṣlāḥī says every inner and outer self is exposed."}, {"id": "40:16/q07/p4", "position": "Their souls stand exposed without bodily veils.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this proposal but rejects it for lacking support from an infallible authority."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q08", "question": "How are the gathered described as clothed or unclothed?", "turns_on": "Different reports qualify the general naked gathering by personal merit or by community.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q08/p1", "position": "People gather barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Bursevī cite a hadith; Abū Ḥayyān adds bare feet and nakedness. Ālūsī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's Prophetic report."}, {"id": "40:16/q08/p2", "position": "Believers who died away from home without fornication receive garments from Paradise.", "reasons": "Bursevī states this exception to the naked gathering."}, {"id": "40:16/q08/p3", "position": "The Prophet's community rises in shrouds, while other communities are barefoot and naked.", "reasons": "Bursevī quotes the Prophet for the community distinction."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q09", "question": "What does 'nothing of them is hidden from Allah' encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase primarily names unrestricted divine knowledge, knowledge for repayment, or the visible emergence of everyone.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q09/p1", "position": "No person, deed, condition, inner secret, or temporal detail escapes God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī adds worldly deeds; Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies thoughts in breasts, al-Qushayrī existing, absent, past, future, impossible and hypothetical events, and al-Biqāʿī outward and inward, now or otherwise. Bursevī cites 69:18; Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes remembered and forgotten things. Ibn ʿĀshūr says minhum embraces the group and their circumstances and shayʾ makes the denial maximally general; Ālūsī expressly chooses this inclusive reading."}, {"id": "40:16/q09/p2", "position": "None of their deeds is hidden, so recompense takes account of every act.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in Ibn al-Jawzī names deeds; al-Māwardī offers God's repayment in knowledge of every deed. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and al-Ṭabrisī also identify deeds and circumstances; al-Wāḥidī adds wealth."}, {"id": "40:16/q09/p3", "position": "No physical screen can hide them, and God brings every person forth.", "reasons": "Qatāda in al-Durr and Ibn al-Jawzī specifies mountains or dwellings; al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī give the alternative that God brings all forth because none is hidden."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q10", "question": "Why emphasize that nothing is hidden when God already knows all?", "turns_on": "The point of specifying the resurrection scene despite God's timeless knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q10/p1", "position": "It explains their exposure and dispels the worldly illusion that concealment from people conceals anything from God.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Bursevī point to imagined walls and screens; al-Bayḍāwī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say the sentence confirms their being exposed. Al-Zamakhsharī links 41:22, 4:108 and 14:48; Ālūsī says this is a resumed explanation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says imagined causes that veiled them are removed."}, {"id": "40:16/q10/p2", "position": "It threatens certain recompense, even though God's knowledge is already complete.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī explicitly calls the wording a threat; al-Māwardī speaks of repayment and Iṣlāḥī says comprehensive exposure leaves no need for witnesses, evidence, excuses, lies or recommendations."}, {"id": "40:16/q10/p3", "position": "God's knowledge is complete at every time, beyond exposed or hidden appearances.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī includes even counterfactual possibilities; Ibn Kathīr says all are equally present in God's knowledge; al-Biqāʿī expressly extends knowledge and power to every day, and Qatāda in al-Durr says nothing is hidden even now."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q11", "question": "How can 'nothing is hidden' function syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause resumes, describes a circumstance, or continues the predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q11/p1", "position": "It is an independent resumed sentence explaining their exposure.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports explanatory resumption; al-Samīn permits independence."}, {"id": "40:16/q11/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause attached to the pronoun in 'exposed.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Ālūsī both list this possibility."}, {"id": "40:16/q11/p3", "position": "It is a second predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Ālūsī both list this possibility."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q12", "question": "What variant wording of 'nothing is hidden' is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q12/p1", "position": "Ubayy's codex adds 'upon Him,' reading that nothing concerning them is hidden from Him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits the codex wording."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q13", "question": "Why name Allah explicitly and say 'of them, anything'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q13/p1", "position": "Allah clarifies a remote antecedent, while minhum and shayʾ extend the negation to all their circumstances.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the antecedent of Allah lies back in the phrase about whom He wills among His servants, with the subject of warn probably the relative pronoun; minhum permits an understood contextual modifier, and shayʾ is maximally general, broader than merely saying no person is hidden."}]}
{"id": "40:16/q14", "question": "When does the question about sovereignty occur?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding exposure and reckoning require a living audience; Rāzī challenges speech addressed to no one, while extinction reports place the declaration before resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q14/p1", "position": "After creation perishes, between the two trumpet blasts, before resurrection.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb in al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī says only the Creator remains and He answers Himself. Ibn ʿUmar calls it the end of worldly time before resurrection; Ibn Kathīr's Trumpet report has God take every soul and ask three times. Al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī and Ibn ʿAbbās in Abū Ḥayyān give the extinction setting; al-Qurṭubī favors the disappearance of every claimant and lineage."}, {"id": "40:16/q14/p2", "position": "At the resurrection gathering, when living people appear before God for judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this alternative. Al-Naḥḥās accepts Ibn Masʿūd's white-plain report and rejects an empty scene. Al-Ṭabrisī prefers it because the verse describes servants leaving graves. Rāzī appeals to the Day of Meeting and adjacent 40:15 and 40:17, saying a speech without a hearer lacks a purpose; believers and unbelievers answer with contrasting feelings. Ibn al-Jawzī says the accounts differ in timing."}, {"id": "40:16/q14/p3", "position": "Before the Hour, a herald announces it to living and dead, and God descends to the lowest heaven for the proclamation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Kathīr and al-Durr; al-Durr says al-Ḥākim authenticated it. Abū Saʿīd's Prophetic report in al-Durr locates the herald between blasts and says the voice reaches living and dead."}, {"id": "40:16/q14/p4", "position": "After humanity perishes, angels may still be present to hear it.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers this accommodation even if the Ibn ʿAbbās extinction report is soundly transmitted."}]}

Rāzī does not prove a unique speaker."}, {"id": "40:16/q15/p3", "position": "God asks, and all creatures answer.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj in al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī says believers and unbelievers answer; Ibn Masʿūd in Ibn ʿAṭiyya says assembled people answer God; al-Ṭabrisī prefers the creatures' answer because they have emerged from graves. {"id": "40:16/q16", "question": "What happens on the white gathering plain?", "turns_on": "Whether the people or the herald provide the answer in the white-plain accounts.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q16/p1", "position": "A caller asks, and the gathered answer, on a white earth like silver.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's account in al-Naḥḥās and Abū Ḥayyān says the white plain resembles silver; al-Naḥḥās accepts it over a question with no creation present. {"id": "40:16/q19", "question": "Why frame exclusive sovereignty as a question and answer?", "turns_on": "Whether the device primarily forces confession, prepares the hearer, or voices what the scene itself displays.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q19/p1", "position": "It compels acknowledgment and humiliates false claimants, while believers rejoice in a truth they confessed.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares a victorious king confronting rebels, answered by speech or state, and cites an unnamed poet's cry after long silence that makes rebels weep blood. {"id": "40:16/q20", "question": "Why single out that day for God's sovereignty?", "turns_on": "Whether the day dramatizes the exposure of false claims at judgment or the literal disappearance of every creature before resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "40:16/q20/p1", "position": "God owns sovereignty always, but worldly pretensions and delegated control vanish or become visibly false that day.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says divine dominion never depends on a time; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says believers already know that creatures lack independent power, while unbelievers then cannot deny it. {"id": "40:60/q04", "question": "What does “Call upon Me” ask people to do?", "turns_on": "Whether duʿāʾ names worship, literal asking, both together, or a specified practice or inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q04/p1", "position": "Worship God alone, affirm His oneness, and obey Him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Zamakhsharī and others cite the following “My worship” and Qurʾānic usage; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the call as tawḥīd, Jarīr as worship, and Biqāʿī includes prayer and other acts of submission. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this a less common figurative use of duʿāʾ; Elmalılı adds practical striving."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p2", "position": "Ask or supplicate to God for needs, with a promised answer.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Mawardī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī state “ask Me and I will give”; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls asking the common literal sense. Rāzī argues the apparent sense needs no shift: supplication itself displays servitude, so refusing it can be pride. Al-Kashf and Ālūsī favor this sense for wording; the surah contrasts arrogant disputation with humble asking (40:69)."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p3", "position": "The command encompasses both asking and worship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says both senses of the shared term operate together, while response likewise covers granting needs and accepting worship. Biqāʿī includes worshipful submission and requests for victory; Elmalılı says prayer and worship entail one another. Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses the terms broadly."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p4", "position": "Remember God and ask Him.", "reasons": "Some interpreters reported by Thaʿlabī, Baghawī and Qurṭubī include remembrance alongside prayer and asking."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p5", "position": "Leave sins, since abandoning disobedience is itself supplication.", "reasons": "Sufyān or al-Thawrī repeatedly answers a request for prayer this way; Ālūsī explains that persistent sin contradicts genuine inward seeking, even after many utterances. Qurṭubī reports it as another explanation; ʿĀʾisha reports prophetic gloss of supplication as seeking forgiveness."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p6", "position": "Obey God so that He grants the response.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's gloss pairs obedience with divine granting."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p7", "position": "Seek God from God, finding Him rather than a requested object.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says finding God yields everything because all things obey His creative command at 36:82; he cites a report that whoever seeks God finds Him. Shiblī's outward exhortation is to invoke God alone, for finding Him is finding everything."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p8", "position": "Respond to God while invoking Him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ reads a reciprocal command: invoke and respond to Me, and I will answer you."}, {"id": "40:60/q04/p9", "position": "Invoke God from desperate need and selfless inward awareness.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq requires utter need and no refuge but God; Shiblī says the inward self must disappear in the unseen and the outward call must be to God alone."}]}
{"id": "40:60/q05", "question": "How is the imperative and its response parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether udʿūnī is an uninflected imperative or jussive after an omitted lām.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q05/p1", "position": "The imperative is uninflected; the response is jussive through an implied condition.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās reports the Basran analysis of udʿūnī, with astajib jussive as the answer; Ālūsī paraphrases: if you call on Me, I answer."}, {"id": "40:60/q05/p2", "position": "The imperative is jussive after a deleted lām; the response is jussive.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās attributes the first analysis to al-Farrāʾ and gives the conditional response analysis for astajib."}]}

{"id": "40:60/q08", "question": "What qualifies or explains the promise to answer prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the unqualified promise is read at face value or in light of divine will, benefit, sincerity and prerequisites.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q08/p1", "position": "God answers according to His will, wisdom, benefit and the request's conditions.", "reasons": "Qushayrī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı cite 6:41 to qualify the open wording; Ṭabrisī says granting a harmful request would be wrong. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ adds humble heart, sincerity, dawn and blessings on Muḥammad."}, {"id": "40:60/q08/p5", "position": "Whoever prays receives a response, and turning to prayer itself opens divine aid.", "reasons": "Anas reports that when God opens prayer He answers; Abū ʿAbd Allāh parallels prayer/answer with gratitude/increase and trust/sufficiency at 14:7 and 65:3. {"id": "40:60/q10", "question": "What status does supplication have as worship?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on supplication itself, its inward humility, or other devotion that can stand in its place.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q10/p1", "position": "Supplication itself is worship, and is among its greatest or best forms.", "reasons": "The Prophet states “supplication is worship” and recites the verse in the Nuʿmān reports; Tirmidhī calls it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ and notes Dharr is trustworthy, while al-Ḥākim calls a chain sound. {"id": "40:60/q12", "question": "Can supplication change a decreed calamity?", "turns_on": "Whether and how the prayer affects an outcome governed by God's knowledge, wisdom or decree.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q12/p1", "position": "Prayer can benefit against calamities already present or yet to come.", "reasons": "Muʿādh explicitly urges prayer for both; Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes open divine promises to transcend ordinary causal expectation."}, {"id": "40:60/q12/p2", "position": "Prayer draws the servant into reliance, while God's wise decree still governs outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Kaʿbī poses the objection that God already does what is best and replies with the benefit of reliance; he says the deterministic objection applies to acts whether known to occur or not. {"id": "40:60/q19", "question": "Why are calling and worship paired in this wording?", "turns_on": "Whether the later clause selects worship, identifies asking as worship, or invites both senses together.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q19/p1", "position": "The later mention of worship explains the earlier command as worship.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī's reading, Zamakhsharī, Baghawī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Kuranyolu use the following clause as proof; Ṭabrisī says calling worship “supplication” makes reward a “response.”"}, {"id": "40:60/q19/p2", "position": "Supplication is itself worship, so proud refusal to ask counts as proud refusal to worship.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues no shift from literal asking is needed; Bayḍāwī and Bursevī explain the warning by treating supplication as a form of worship; Ālūsī prefers asking since it requires fewer figurative moves. {"id": "40:60/q25", "question": "How does the verse's warning work rhetorically?", "turns_on": "Whether the second clause chiefly gives the reason for the command or sharpens the equivalence of prayer and worship.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q25/p1", "position": "The warning explains and reinforces the command to call.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the relative clause hints at the command's reason and the Hell warning deters idol worship; Biqāʿī says pride often causes abandonment of prayer. {"id": "40:60/q26", "question": "How do descriptions of Hell deepen the warning?", "turns_on": "Distinct reported images of Hell's severity.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q26/p1", "position": "An iron shackle from Hell would crush a mountain to the black water.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Razzāq reports the statement from Ibn al-Taymī's father."}, {"id": "40:60/q26/p2", "position": "Arrogant people are confined in Hell's prison and made to drink foul fluid.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports their resurrection as tiny human forms, covered in humiliation, then confinement in Bulas under fire."}]}
{"id": "40:60/q27", "question": "What neighboring reports or technical discussions accompany this verse?", "turns_on": "Which ancillary report or linguistic example a source includes in its discussion.", "positions": [{"id": "40:60/q27/p1", "position": "Reports about the Dajjāl's duration and warning are transmitted nearby.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports Ibn Masʿūd's forty mornings and successive day lengths of a Friday, month and year; ʿUbayd reports wrath against followers who join for sustenance; Ashʿath's father reports Ibn Masʿūd warning against rumor as decree may arrive faster."}, {"id": "40:60/q27/p2", "position": "A divine report combines exclusive worship, reward, answered prayer and reciprocal goodwill.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Abū Yaʿlā transmits the report of four matters from the Prophet's Lord."}, {"id": "40:60/q27/p3", "position": "General grammatical examples of relative clauses, articles and genitives are discussed.", "reasons": "Itqān treats the relative clause here as general; in adjacent general examples it classifies definite articles by known referent, exhaustive inclusion and genus, and genitives by concision, exaltation and generality, citing 15:42, 39:7 and 24:63; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses chosen servants in the cited examples."}, {"id": "40:60/q27/p4", "position": "Adjacent verses have alternative conjunction and predication analyses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the conjunction before lākin an embellishment; for the later “Allah” he offers apposition to “your Lord,” or several subject/predicate parses, preferring a fresh explanatory sentence because it suits the creation argument and exposes ingratitude (40:64). {"id": "41:39/q03", "question": "How is “that you see the earth humbled” parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q03/p1", "position": "The an-clause is a nominative subject, with khāshiʿa a circumstantial accusative; an implicit governing verb is supplied where a clause cannot begin independently.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports Sībawayh’s nominative subject analysis despite his usual bar on beginning with an, gives his own ḥāl analysis for khāshiʿa, and reports al-Māzinī’s estimated kayfa istaqarra Zayd as an example of supplying a governing verb. ʿAbd al-Qāhir says coordinated clauses forming a condition must be parsed as a grammatical whole."}]}
